RydAR/RydAR for iPhone

RydAR for iPhone

A heads-up for the next bend.

RydAR is an iPhone co-pilot for tight bends in Arkansas. It uses the road ahead and a curve database bundled in the app to speak a suggested speed before a curve.

Join the free TestFlight beta ↗

Spoken curve warnings

A warning can say, “Slow to 25 mph for the curve ahead.” The spoken number uses the low end of the calculated range, rounded down. Confidently matched bends on the same named road can share a “Curves ahead” warning, with a separate warning for a notably sharper bend.

The app normally looks about 12 seconds ahead, with a warning distance between 100 and 450 meters. It skips a warning when there is too little road left to act on it, or when the car is already moving away from the bend. See how curve matching and suggested speeds work.

Curve data available without loading the website

The curve database ships inside the iPhone app. A drive does not wait for the website to load or fetch its curve map. GPS reception and a confident road match still matter; if location fixes stop for more than four seconds, the drive screen reports the gap.

RydAR covers Arkansas. Its bundled inventory does not add a belt of roads in neighboring states. The public Arkansas curve map lets you explore county-road bends before setting out.

Driver and Teen driver modes

Driver mode shows the curve information and supports an optional camera road-surface check. Teen driver mode speaks the same numeric curve advisories, vibrates twice before each one, and lets the screen sleep. Teen driver mode has no camera, curve display, or Live Activity.

Set up the trip while parked. Suggested speeds do not replace posted signs, attention to the road, or your judgment about conditions.

Try the beta

RydAR is currently distributed through Apple TestFlight. Open the RydAR beta invitation on your iPhone and follow Apple’s installation steps. A beta can change and availability depends on TestFlight.

Read about camera frames and optional anonymous sharing. The RydAR source code is public, and you can report an issue on GitHub.
